speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since it is late I shall be very brief.
First, I should like to say that I would have voted for the abolition of capital punishment if, in the first place, Parliament had provided for as long a debate on all the ways and means to ensure real social reform concerning the judicial system, the penitentiaries, the rehabilitation and re-education of those living on the fringe of society.
IMr. Simpson.]
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Second, if parliament had committed itself to amend the Criminal Code, more particularly chapter 217, Prisons and Reformatories Act; chapter 206, Penitentiary Act; chapter 307, Canada Evidence Act; as well as chapter 264, Parole Act and chapter 160, Juvenile Delinquents Act.
Third, if parliament undertook to amend section 660 of the Criminal Code with regard to habitual criminals, because I am convinced that if the Criminal Code were amended to read "shall" instead of "may", society would be spared many murders.
As an example, I should like to quote from a talk given by Mr. J. P. Gilbert, police director of the city of Montreal, before the Ste. Marie alumni association. I quote:
To give a concrete illustration of the problem of habitual criminals, I wanted to quote figures, he said. I have examined the record of every individual involved in murder cases in Montreal, during the last fifteen months, a total of 30 individuals involved in some 20 murder cases.
I had taken from the record what is called the "tally sheet" of these people. This sheet shows in chronological order, the offences committed since age 18. The number of offences on the sheet varies according to each individual from a minimum of four offences to a maximum of 46, the last noted being a charge of murder, some sort of crowning glory for their career.
Those thirty persons have a total of 359 offences charged against them.
Each tally sheet was examined and a line drawn at the exact point where the criminal careers of those individuals should have ended, because they became habitual criminals under the law.
Now, and that is the most important thing, if at the proper time we had put an end to the criminal activities of those people through preventive detention, and if they had been given an indeterminate sentence, we would most likely have prevented, not only 20 murders, but also 16 robberies and 219 criminal and other offences, for a total of 255 offences.
The legislator has provided for the use of an indeterminate sentence in the very case we are dealing with.
It is our responsibility to make sure, in the best interests of society, that the law becomes operative. It is with a view to social protection, not for a purely vengeful purpose, that the Montreal police department intends to bring before the courts in the near future all individuals who, under the act, are habitual criminals. It is in the light of this and for the same reason that we are looking forward to obtaining the support of all parts of this society which it is our duty to protect.
In the fourth place, I would vote for abolition of capital punishment if I were given the assurance that the accused persons shall be given an equal chance. The crown should try to get to the truth much more than to have a man convicted, as may happen in some cases.

For this, I suggest that the crown make available to the defence free of charge, instruments at his own disposal, that is detectives, investigators, experts in various fields.
In the fifth place, if we could provide our society with true and efficient means of rehabilitation, especially for the prevention of crime, this would mean that we should set up throughout our country re-education programs teaching what is right. Hon. Cyrille Vaillancourt stated recently in this connection:
What is the use of re-educating those who live on the fringe of society if, on the other hand, they are taught evil.
"In conscience," say the abolitionists. Hence, I shall say that if there were judicial errors, as has been argued many times, but this has never been proved-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Messrs. Byrne, Nugent, Scott (Danforth) and Stanbury:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Criminal Code for the purpose of
(a)	abolishing the death penalty in respect of all offences under that act;
(b)	substituting a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment in those cases where the death penalty is now mandatory; and
(c)	providing that no person upon whom a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment is imposed shall be released from imprisonment without the prior approval of the Governor in Council.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speeches we have heard in this debate have been of a uniformly high order and have shown a great deal of thought on the part of hon. members. One could single out any number of speeches touching on both sides of the question for particular mention. I think of the very good speech made by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier). I did not agree with him but it was an exceedingly well prepared and well thought out speech. The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) also made a very eloquent plea. I did not agree with him either but I think he gave a particularly fine demonstration of spontaneous speaking in the house. We also heard from, among others, the hon. member for Queens, and this afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) spoke. Those are the ones I remember but perhaps it is invidious of me to mention them because I am sure I have missed some very good ones.
I had hoped to rise earlier this afternoon to indicate that I was opposed to the amendment and rise now to indicate that I am also opposed to the motion. I do not think that I am going to bring to the attention of hon. members any new argument one way or the other but I do feel, like all other hon. members, that this question is one which affects us personally. It is not one which was a matter of electoral campaigning. It is not a matter of political partisanship or party platform, and thank goodness it is not. Therefore one must explain one's view to one's constituents.
Right from the outset I would want to reject any impatience that has been shown by certain editorial writers or by some speakers
April 5. 1966

in the house who, either because they have written articles or have spoken in the house and come to their own conclusion, feel that this debate should now end, particularly if other speakers in this house want to express a view which is contrary to the decision arrived at by these editorial writers or other speakers in the house. I can only classify that as some form of intellectual or moral arrogance and frankly it is more to be pitied than criticized.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I am against the resolution as I was against the amendment. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), and others I feel that the burden of proof in effecting a change in the law is upon those who seek to change the law. This may be my feeling as a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, and I confess that so far their arguments have not been compelling enough to effect a change in the law as it now stands in the statutes.
I know that everyone has expressed his views bona fide one way or the other. I have a folder full of letters and petitions on both sides of the question. I would thank the people in my constituency and those elsewhere who have written me on the subject, and I am only sorry that I cannot agree with them all. But they have written to me according to their conscience, and I am speaking and voting today, I hope, according to my conscience.
I do not think that at this time there is any purpose in canvassing the argument whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent. However, the argument usually made to us to indicate that capital punishment is not a deterrent is that those people who have been apprehended and sentenced to death and questioned on the subject have said that it was no deterrent to them. But, Mr. Speaker, as indicated earlier this afternoon, there may be hundreds and thousands of men and women in this country who have been deterred. These people do not appear in any statistics. In the same way there may be thousands of men who have been deterred from committing armed robbery or any other form of crime simply because there is a punishment for that crime. If I may say so, I think the argument that capital punishment is not a deterrent puts in doubt the whole theory of punishment because it applies merely to what you might call the peak and not to the whole slope of the theory of punishment.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
When we get to the very bottom of the slope we may look at the three or four-year
Criminal Code
old who will not raid the cookie barrel or the jam pot because he knows that if he does so without permission his little backside will be warmed or he will be slapped on the hand. That deterrent fear is fundamental to the theory of punishment and in my example we see it at its most elementary stage. I know that some people think it is wrong to punish three and four-year olds because this might create repressions in the child I will leave those people to their own opinions. In any event, that is my comment with regard to the theory of capital punishment not being a deterrent.
I must also pay attention to the views of the people who are charged in this country with the protection of society and the enforcement of the law. I disagree with some of them on many things at times but in this regard I pay attention to them. Our police forces have had far more experience than many of us in dealing with that segment of society which unfortunately runs afoul of the law.
Also, when we cast aside entirely the opinions of the Attorneys General of this country and the opinions of their officials who have the responsibility for administering criminal law, we are arrogating unto ourselves some sort of exclusive preserve with regard to the theory of the definition of the law of punishment or of criminal law in this country. We know that the majority of Attorneys General in this country have pronounced themselves in favour of retaining capital punishment. Their views are not to be cast aside and denigrated. The Attorneys General and their staffs are part of the lawmaking process and they have their right to opinions about capital punishment.
Another reason, Mr. Speaker, why I should not like to see capital punishment abolished is, frankly, that the abolition of the death penalty would reduce murder to the level of many lesser crimes in the mind of society. Let us look briefly at some crimes for which life imprisonment is the maximum sentence and for which crimes life sentences have been given. Those crimes include rape, abortion, robbery with violence, and treason which is punishable not only with life imprisonment but in the alternative with death. A habitual criminal who has been found guilty of at least three indictable offences may also be sentenced to life imprisonment. Is it intended to bring murder down to this more prosaic level? Murder is the most abominable crime against a human being. After all, we as

April 5. 1966
Criminal Code
humans have an inalienable right not to be deprived unlawfully of our lives.
May I quote briefly from the White Paper on capital punishment prepared by the Department of Justice. I quote a passage taken from the report of United Kingdom royal commission which sat from 1959 to 1963. As found on page 2 of this pamphlet it reads:
-We think it is reasonable to suppose that the deterrent force of capital punishment operates not only by affecting the conscious thoughts of individuals tempted to commit murder, but also by building up in the community, over a long period of time, a deep feeling of peculiar abhorrence for the crime of murder. "The fact that men are hung for murder is one great reason why murder is considered so dreadful a crime." This widely diffused effect on the moral consciousness of society is impossible to assess, but it must be at least as important as any direct part which the death penalty may play as a deterrent in the calculations of potential murderers. It is likely to be specially potent in this country, where the punishment for lesser offences is much more lenient than in many other countries, and the death penalty stands out in the sharper contrast.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what was applicable to Great Britain in 1963 is today equally applicable to Canada.
May I now state my last reason why I would vote against the motion. I particularly refer to paragraph 3 thereof. It is my feeling that over a period of years the executive has improperly usurped power by setting itself up as a sort of super grand jury to examine every death sentence. These examinations are held under varying conditions. Cabinet may be dominated by two or three strongminded individuals whose personal views on capital punishment then become, by an indirect process, the law of the land. We do not know what quorums attend cabinet meetings, we do not know what members attend, we do not know what forms of pressure, political and otherwise, are going on in cabinet under certain conditions. These things are all in my mind. No reasons are ever published why a death sentence was or was not carried out.
However, by being critical of what is being done by the executive I do not subscribe to the view that this argument should be used against the retention of capital punishment. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I find it exceedingly strange that the present cabinet, without the sanction of the electorate, without the sanction of parliament, has by its own actions deformed the law. That law was passed by parliament which has the supreme authority to do so. It was not passed by cabinet, because parliament has supreme authority in this country. Cabinet has deformed

by its actions the law which a good number of those present in the house passed when the Criminal Code was amended in 1961 to create two classes of murder, capital and non-capital.
My criticism of this wholesale intrusion by cabinet into the carrying out of the death penalty as laid down by law and with the safeguards now provided is that it is wrong. Except in exceptional cases where there may have been a recommendation for clemency, cabinet intrusion has been wrong.
I think that the provision in paragraph (c) of the resolution that parole from a life sentence shall be subject to review by cabinet is wrong. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that every stricture I have made against cabinet action regarding interference with the death penalty is applicable also to parole.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Political pressures can be very prevalent. I know this has happened. The position would not be made public. Who can appear before cabinet to make representations? It is the rights of individuals that are being made the subject of secretive consideration and decision.
I would much prefer that we have a parole board of experts charged with the authority for release from a life sentence. In the same way the carrying out of the death penalty should be on the recommendation of the equivalent of the Home Secretary, the Solicitor General, let us say, who with his staff would make the review, and unless there were extraordinary circumstances there should not be interference by individual members of the cabinet with respect to the decision.
In conclusion may I say that I think the law as amended in 1961 should be given a much fairer trial. It had only two years of application before de facto the death penalty was abolished by what I say was an improper action of the executive in deforming the law, perhaps not the letter of the law but certainly the spirit of the law, without any sanction from parliament.
This sanction from parliament, this law and these amendments we are considering must also be considered by the other place which is also part of parliament and whose views in this regard must also be consulted. Therefore I would urge hon. members to reject the resolution.

speechtext: Without being partisan may I say that the hon. gentleman is a little touchy because my strictures did not refer to any particular administration except that I said this administration had de facto abolished capital punishment. Under the previous administration there was capital punishment but it was restricted from what it was prior to 1961 because prior to 1961 you could have had a case like Truscott which could not arise under the law today. On this point I say that if the cap fits it may be put on. I am speaking personally. I am expressing my own views and I am not putting any partisan tag on any of my strictures.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the resolution because one of the experiences that has agonized me throughout the years is the fact that the most serious crime in the Criminal Code of this country requires the least proof for conviction. In fact, more positive proof is required to obtain conviction of a person who might go into a five cent to a dollar store and pick a dollar item off the counter. The proof necessary to convict would have to be positive in that case whereas in the case of murder, which seldom has witnesses, we proceed by making proof through circumstantial evidence.
Notwithstanding the fact that I favour the abolition of capital punishment I would make a distinction in the case of policemen and prison guards. I would reconcile that with the theory that when I am asleep in my bed at night and a policeman is on his beat protecting me and exposing his life to danger who feels he needs the protection of the deterrent of capital punishment, I think I owe him the protection that he feels he needs in order to protect me. I would also make that distinction with respect to prison guards because if a convicted murderer is condemned to prison for life and then kills a prison guard he will have committed a second murder for which there is no punishment.
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) said that we also have to examine the question of the definition of insanity. I agree with that but we also have to go into the question of how confessions are obtained. It is all very well for us to say in criticism of
Criminal Code
confessions obtained in the Soviet Union that they are the result of brainwashing whereas confessions obtained in Canada are quite all right. In this connection there are many avenues of the Criminal Code that we should consider in a civilized society.
One of the most abnormal things we do under our code is to charge a man who has attempted suicide with a criminal offence. I think it is wrong to take a person who is addicted to opium and throw him in a penitentiary, because he is obviously sick just as the person who attempts suicide is obviously sick.
It has been said that capital punishment should be retained for fiendish crimes. I would say that the more sadistic the crime the less responsible is the person who perpetrates it because that person is obviously sick. When I support abolishing capital punishment it is not because I want to do it for the sake of the person who has committed murder but rather for the purpose of raising the level of our own civilization because if capital punishment is not abolished today in Canada it will be abolished at some time in the future.
Recently I received a pamphlet circulated by the Communist Party of Canada which through a press release has asked the public and members of parliament to support the abolition of capital punishment. I would say to the Communist Party of Canada that I am supporting the abolition of capital punishment, but I would ask them to print 200 million copies of their pamphlet and distribute them in the Soviet Union where the authorities are still executing people for economic crimes.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The other day I saw, as did many hon. members, an execution that took place in full view of the public in Saigon. It was for an economic crime and it was a revolting sight. It did not act as a deterrent in Saigon, because the people of Saigon have revolted against the sight of this execution and now have demanded that the military government of South Viet Nam be replaced by a civilian government.
I do not advocate it, Mr. Speaker, but it would be interesting to speak about the manner in which the Bible has been brought into the question of whether we should retain or abolish capital punishment. It would be interesting-and again I am not advocating it-if back to back with the debate we are now having on the abolition of capital punishment

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
we had a debate on euthanasia. If that were to occur we would have the retentionists going to the abolitionists and saying "Lend me your notes because tomorrow I am speaking on euthanasia", and the abolitionists would be going to the retentionists and saying, "Give me your notes because tomorrow I am speaking on euthanasia".
I am not going to quote Biblical texts, but if I were to quote Biblical texts it would seem to me that the one instance in which God sat as the judge in Biblical history and heard the case of the first murderer he called the accused before him, sat as the judge, heard the case and condemned the accused, but he did not condemn him to execution. He condemned him to what Cain described as punishment greater than he could bear.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask-when I am speaking in this manner it is a question of one civilization versus another-what kind of a civilization do we want to live in? I am convinced that the rehabilitation of criminals will not be brought about through psychiatry. Incidentally, I feel that psychiatry has failed in rehabilitation, one field in which it could have shown its worth. I do not believe rehabilitation lies in psychiatry. I do not believe it lies in sociology or in the probation officer. I think it lies in chemistry. In the future we will treat a criminal as we treat a person today who has diabetes. The chemical imbalance which exists in the criminal and which makes him a Mr. Hyde instead of a Dr. Jekyll will be found.
I should like to quote an article which appeared in Time magazine, the issue of February 25, 1966. It reads as follows:
In general, drug control of personality will be widely accepted well before the year 2000. If a wife or husband seems to be unusually grouchy on a given evening, says Rand's Olaf Helmer, a spouse will be able to pop down to the corner drugstore, buy some anti-grouch pills, and slip them into the coffee. Or a lackadaisical person could be dosed into a sense of ambition. Electrical stimulus of brain areas has been shown to produce responses of fear, affection, laughter or sex arousal; such techniques, says Yale's Dr. Jose Delgado, "will certainly increase man's ability to influence the behavior of man".
If this be true, if it is only a matter of chemistry, then it indicates how uncivilized we are in this century to continue with the death penalty.
So, Mr. Speaker, with the expose I have made I should like to move an amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme), which is in

line with the type of amendment he moved. It reads as follows:
That the motion be amended
(1)	by adding to paragraph (a) of the motion the words "except the capital murder of a police officer, prison guard or other person as described in subparagraph (i) or (ii) of paragraph (c) of subsection (2) of section 202A of the Criminal Code"; and
(2)	by adding to paragraph (b) of the motion the words "except in the case of the capital murder of a police officer, prison guard or other person as described in subparagraph (i) or (Ii) of paragraph (c) of subsection (2) of section 202A of the Code"; and
(3)	by inserting in paragraph (c) of the motion immediately after the word "imposed", the words "or in respect of whom a sentence of death is commuted".
In conclusion I should like to say that the history of man has been a history of killing, but perhaps if we abolish capital punishment and every country in the world abolishes capital punishment wars in the future will be averted.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to some very fine speeches in the house on the pros and cons of capital punishment. Members have spoken with sincerity on both sides of the question. Sincere men can look at the same problem and have different answers. I did not support the five-year plan simply because we would have little if any more information than we should have today after four years of abolition. We do not have the personnel in psychiatry or in psychology to carry on in depth the studies required. Considering that in this country we have had four years when no one has been hanged and considering that only a five-year period was sought, I could not in all conscience vote for that type of resolution.
If the main resolution carries the government will have to present a bill in the house. I hope that at that stage it will be referred to a committee where witnesses can be called and where first-hand information can be obtained from those dealing with murderers. I mean psychiatrists whose practices have involved this type of prisoner over the last ten years, psychologists who have studied these prisoners, some of the penal officials who deal daily with those who have committed murders, and some police officers who are concerned with law enforcement and crime.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
We could also receive first-hand opinions from members of the John Howard Society, which has such a great reputation for working over the years in the interest of criminals,
April 5, 1966

in an attempt to rehabilitate them. Perhaps we should also hear the opinions of parole officers who work daily with these people, and police officers who have handled them over the years. Finally, perhaps we should hear information and opinions from penal officials who have worked with these people in these institutions and know of their shortcomings and good points. It is only by this method that we can decide fairly and honestly how to deal with the situation.
It seems to me that we are considering this whole situation from the wrong end of the scale. We should go back in case histories and find out why these people become murderers. We must go back and study the lives of the boys and girls in Canada who, after 15 or 20 years, commit murder. This is the target at which we should direct our sights. If we can prevent crime we will not have murder, and there will be no need for debates such as the kind in which we are now involved. In other areas we use preventatives rather than curatives, and I suggest this is the answer to the present problem.
At this time I should like to refer to certain figures regarding the number of individuals paroled. I think the average runs in the neighbourhood of 60 per cent, of whom approximately 95 per cent require some kind of supervision. I believe 50 per cent of those either requiring a little or a lot of supervision eventually return to prison. Mr. Speaker, I note that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) is shaking his head. If he has anything to tell the house I should like him to do so because the figures I have cited are those I have taken from medical records and journals available to me.
It is interesting to note that in Canada we have on the average one parole officer for every 60 parolees. This figure is very poor when compared to the comparable figure in countries which have studied this whole problem and have obtained the best results. On the average they have one parole officer for every 25 parolees.
I suggest there is no value in a five-year trial period because we cannot in that time train the number of psychiatrists and other personnel necessary to a successful evaluation of the rehabilitative program in that period of time. If we do away with capital punishment we will be faced with one of two facts. We will either have our penitentiaries inhabited by people who have been sentenced to life imprisonment or we will have to develop successful rehabilitation measures.
Criminal Code
One might be led to believe by the motion now before us that individuals convicted of murder would be kept in prison for a considerable period of time, until pardoned by the cabinet. However, if one considers the recard of the last four years he will realize that the cabinet will parole them all. It would be far more cruel to incarcerate an individual for the rest of his life than it would be quietly to put him out of the way. If we put these people in a prison for the rest of their lives and wash our hands of them they will gradually deteriorate in mind and body. I am sure if hon. members had an opportunity to talk to some of these people they would soon learn that fact.
Has our science of analysis and assessment reached a point that we can honestly decide which convicted murderers can be rehabilitated and safely put back into society? One need only refer to the records to come to the conclusion that we have not reached that point. I know of one particular case where a psychiatrist let a man out of the penitentiary on his belief that the prisoner had been rehabilitated and would become a good useful citizen. Within a year of his release he murdered four young boys.
These are the shocking things that one must consider in deciding in good conscience what should be done. We are unable to decide without doubt whether or not an individual who is allowed out of prison on parole is going to commit another crime. I remember the case of an individual who escaped from penitentiary. He had been confined there as a result of a conviction for armed robbery. He was recaptured, returned to the prison and considered to be one of the worst prisoners in that penitentiary. At one point he was confined to the black hole. After a period of time the people responsible considered that he had been rehabilitated. In passing perhaps I should state that this man moved step by step from being considered the worst criminal in the penitentiary to one having the highest position of trust, meriting permission to work in the library. Everyone agreed that he had been completely rehabilitated and should be released. The psychiatrist, his pastor and jail officials all believed this to be the fact. His case was presented to parliament through a petition and he was eventually released.
Following this man's release he travelled around the country addressing service and boys' clubs, giving them very good advice. It was strange, however, that within six months of his release a series of crimes occurred

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
throughout central Ontario. Eventually this man was caught in the act of robbing a liquor store in western Ontario and in the attempted capture of him he was shot and killed. It is perhaps interesting to note that the crime wave then ceased.
I have just brought this case to the attention of hon. members as an indication that we cannot know absolutely and as a certainty what is in the mind of a criminal, or what he might do following his release. That is the situation which confronts us at this time.
In Canada today we have over 100,000 prisoners in our jails and penitentiaries, and it is said to cost in the neighbourhood of $20,000 to $25,000 per year to maintain these prisoners and assist in the maintenance of their families, while insuring the enforcement of the law, I suggest that is not an exaggerated figure when one considers the cost of maintaining families and providing police forces across the country. It does not take much of a mathematician to figure out that it costs approximately $2 billion per year as a result of the incarceration of the 100,000 prisoners now in our jails.
At this time we are acutely short of parole officers and psychiatrists. This parliament should begin to consider the major and overall problem of penal reform. We should do something to find out where crime really begins. I mention this with some feeling because we must go back and find out what drives these young people into a life of crime. We should not be using our time to consider hanging, but rather we should be devoting our energy, time and money to research in the field of crime.
In conclusion, it is my earnest belief that we should refer this whole problem to a committee in order that we can obtain the opinion of the experts regarding this whole matter. Having done that, we might be in a position to make an honest decision as to what is best for the individuals who have been unfortunate enough to have committed murder.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not speak previously in this debate because I thought that the White Paper prepared by the Department of Justice put before the house in a very satisfactory way the arguments on both sides of this vital question. In addition, those who have spoken, as several hon. members have commented, have approached this difficult question in a serious and earnest manner. In other words, sir, I felt that the arguments which would determine whether I should vote for or against the main motion had been adequately explored.
This evening however something happened. The hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Klein) put before the house a most important amendment. In doing this he was following in the direction set the other evening by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme). The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency had the misfortune to discover that his amendment was out of order. This evening the hon. member for Cartier has revived the substance of that amendment in a manner which I assume is in order.
In examining this complicated question of capital punishment, which has excited the earnest consideration of some of the most profound people of our western civilization for the last 200 years, I do not think it is correct to turn to what one might call "principles", in the hope that there one will find adequate guidance for the conclusion one should draw. We do not live in a perfect world; consequently, the principles that we sometimes discuss in an academic way, the principles we find set forth in books on philosophy, do not help us too much when we are confronted with practical situations. Therefore, sir, I do not find the arguments based on "principle" adduced on either side of this question helpful or conclusive.
It seems to me that we have to proceed in a much more pragmatic way. I do not mind telling you, sir, that if I had a plain choice between the retention of capital punishment and its abolition, my judgment would lead me to vote in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. I would be hard put, in defending that judgment, to marshal data or
April 5, 1966

theoretical argument that would inevitably lead to that conclusion. Similarly, I think if I were arguing for the opposite judgment I would have the same difficulty. I do not believe that data or theoretical argument point to the judgment one ought to make.
In other words, I believe that one makes up one's mind on a question such as this chiefly by turning to all one's past experience, to all the practical cases that one has lived with throughout his life. I am saying that my own experience, such as it is, would lead me to favour the abolition of capital punishment, and I am quite prepared to insist that there are other members in this house whose experience would lead them to a different conclusion. These are the facts of life; and I think we ought to explain how we reach our conclusion in a realistic way and not by disguising our human fallibility behind an insistence that someone has conferred upon us, in this particular matter, principles which are certain and sure. While I am in favour of the abolition of capital punishment, I recognize that there are people who feel very strongly that those people whose task it is to defend our society and state from those who would destroy those institutions, namely those we often call "officers of the peace," ought to be specially protected.
I do not think it is inconsistent with my general inclination toward the abolition of capital punishment to support the amendment that the hon. member for Cartier has put before the house. His amendment is couched in legal language, and I had to turn to the Criminal Code to see what it was all about. I find that section 202A of the Criminal Code provides, in subsection (c), that murder is capital murder in respect of any person who by his own act caused or assisted in causing the death of "a police officer, police constable, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, acting in the course of his duties." It goes on to say that murder is capital murder in the case where a person causes the death of "a warden, deputy warden, instructor, keeper, gaoler, guard or other officer or permanent employee of a prison, acting in the course of his duties."
The effect of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cartier would be to modify the resolution put before the house so that the penalty for capital murder as now prescribed in the law would continue to apply to cases where individuals killed persons as
Criminal Code
described in the subsections of section 202A of the Criminal Code which I have just read. It seems to me that to accept this amendment is perfectly logical. I am in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. I realize that my judgment is quite fallible. I realize there are those who feel strongly that capital punishment should be retained for those who kill these classes of persons, and I am prepared to yield to their superior experience in this regard. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Cartier deserves my support and, I would hope, the support of other hon. members.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many hon. members I shall deal only briefly with the question before us, one of the most important that we have to settle.
To this end, I shall avoid the figures of speech used by some of my colleagues in discussing this resolution, so that I may examine the problem with all the possible objectivity.
I shall also stay away from the emotional style, so that emotions will not replace the logic that should guide us when we are trying to determine whether capital punishment should be removed from or retained in our statutes.
Mr. Speaker, in order to determine whether capital punishment should be removed from or retained in our statutes in cases of capital murder, I think one should restrict oneself to the value of the expression "capital murder" or, if you wish, "premeditated murder".
To begin with, let me say that I probably lack the qualifications of a lawyer to deal with this matter, but with all the respect I can feel for members of the legal profession, I suggest it would be advisable to let those who practise law in a professional way assess the value of the resolution.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, a premeditated criminal offence is devoid of all passion that could lessen the guilt of the offender. Such an act is committed viciously, in a dastardly fashion, when fully aware of the causes and effects, both for the victim or victims and the culprit or culprits. It is committed either for easy profit or to eliminate a person who might interfere with the illegitimate plans of a murderer.
Faced with such a situation, what is the responsibility and the duty of society toward those who set it up for their own protection?

April 5. 1966
Criminal Code
In my opinion, this is the question which members of the house must answer: What is the responsibility and the duty of society toward those who set it up for their own protection? Responsibility, duty, obligation are imperatives which legitimate authorities must carry out with promptness, firmness and justice.
Promptness must in no way lessen prudence; neither must firmness prevent understanding, nor slackness replace justice. Dura lex, sed lex is a saying well known to our lawyers and which expresses very well the heavy responsibliity entrusted to those vested with the duty and the obligation of enforcing the law.
We all realize the great responsibility that rests with us in this debate, that of deciding whether or not we should maintain in our statutes the death penalty for a person guilty of capital murder.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) said yesterday something amounting to this: When an execution takes place, we all feel involved. Yes indeed, how could it be otherwise since it rests with us to make the decisions required in the matter of law enforcement and protection of society?
When a soldier, as member of a firing squad, has to shoot point-blank a comrade in arms, does he not feel much more directly involved? Yet, he has to go through with it. It is his duty.
Our society is under the same obligation to do its duty.
To my mind, it is not, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North has said, a question of whether it is right or wrong for us to take a human life but whether the elimination of the author or authors of a capital murder is the only means to ensure the protection we are bound to give society.
Such is the question we must ask of ourselves, and not the question put by the hon. member for Winnipeg North who, to my mind, is defending the objective by which we must be guided in discussing the merits of this resolution.
That, I feel, is the cornerstone of the decision the house is called upon to render.
May I be permitted to quote, as an example, a commentary recently published in Le Devoir, by Mr. Claude Wagner, Minister of Justice of the province of Quebec, former judge and a highly reputable lawyer when he

was in private practice. Here is what Mr. Wagner said:
At a time when crime is on the increase and when greater efforts are being made to fight all types of crime, especially organized crime, it is hardly necessary to underline the naivety that would be shown by the Parliament of Canada should it decide to abolish capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, if the death penalty is not a preventive, it is undoubtedly the sole protection of the community against repetition of the offence.
He who deprives another of the right to live forfeits himself that right.
At this point, one can rightfully ask questions which we must of necessity answer.
Would the abolition of the death penalty for capital murder give society the protection it is entitled to?
Does our society have means of protection against the murderer as efficient as the death penalty?
Is the sentence of death decreed against the murderer by society to be interpreted as a deterrent or as a vindictive act?
Is the society that frees a murderer more civilized than the one that does away with him?
What is the greatest risk for our society, that of hanging an innocent man by retaining capital punishment or that of endangering the life of honest citizens by abolishing capital punishment?
The first hypothesis is unlikely, since the legal precautions with which the judicial system has been surrounded in the last few years leave very little chance of hanging an innocent man by mistake.
As for the second hypothesis, Mr. Speaker, it will obviously remain as long as we leave potential murderers at liberty.
How many of the abolitionists would be willing to live with a reprieved murderer? The abolitionists might find the answer to this question disappointing.
Why? Because none of the possible volunteers would feel safe and agree to the experiment.
It is up to the authorities to ensure the greatest possible safety for the individual by all the means at their disposal, that is by legislation and its enforcement through delegated authority.
Of course, our society is deficient in its ways of preventing crime. Therefore, we should ask ourselves whether our society is
April 5. 1966

taking every social, economic and educational step to eliminate as much as possible the causes of crime.
In this respect, we certainly have urgent, imperative and immediate responsibilities.
Murderers do not always come from the poor classes. Some belong to the upper classes of society. But criminals undoubtedly most often spring from among the poverty-stricken.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
That is why I deplore the time devoted by the house to the matter of deciding whether or not we should abolish capital punishment, and that a period of time has never been devoted to a substantial debate on the means to fight human destitution in our country.
The pity shown the criminals would be better justified if it were shown the parents of murder victims or the poverty-stricken.
While waiting for this change of objective, it is our duty to point out clearly what primarily is the role of the legally constituted authority in our democratic society.
This role seems clear to me. It consists in giving every honest and law-abiding Canadian citizen the assurance to be able to enjoy fully his right to life, without danger of being deprived of it by anyone.
Those who, by their actions, act contrary to this basic and undeniable premise, must expect society to deal most severely with them.
This protection sometimes, unfortunately, entails the elimination of the guilty person from our society.
That is why I must in my conscience vote for the retention of the death penalty in our statutes, so that society does not consider itself forsaken by those who have been given a mandate to protect it.
Concerning the amendment moved by the member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) and the other moved by the member for Cartier (Mr. Klein), I think the first one changes nothing to the situation now existing in Canada, since the cabinet can, by decision, commute all death sentences handed down.
Concerning the amendment moved by the member for Cartier, I believe it has some merit, but it falls short of what is required, since it seems to be concerned tremendously, and justly so, with the policemen, the person in authority, but very little with the protection of the individual, of society which gave us, as I said a while ago, the mandate to protect it against actions deserving the most
Criminal Code
rigorous punishment. Let us try, Mr. Speaker, to build a society for law-abiding people, a society in which potential criminals, these parasites of society, will be aware of the consequences of their actions.
Why should legislation announce with fanfare to potential murderers that the Canadian parliament is considering their iniquities and is ready to absolve them at the first opportunity.
I think we must today take an extremely important decision, binding our conscience. I know and I believe that every member will fulfil this responsibility with justice and objectivity, for the good of his fellow citizens and his voters, the taxpayers who send them here to speak on their behalf.
Personally, I take my stand. I am conscious of discharging my duty and reflecting here the opinion of my constituents.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few suggestions which should be taken into serious consideration by this government.
I suggest that we should revise and put teeth in our legislation against crime in Canada; that we should control more adequately the sale of fire-arms and restrict it to specially authorized organizations.
I believe also that we should spend a lot of time in the house discussing the ways and means of improving the circumstances of human beings in our country and contributing to the rehabilitation of poor families in Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I agree with those who suggested, in the course of this debate, that a fund should be instituted in order to help the families of murder victims.
I believe that this request, which was made by the Quebec Federation of Municipal Policemen, is worthwhile and that the government should take it into consideration as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if, in previous discussions, reference was made in the house to a telegram sent by the Quebec Federation of Municipal Policemen, which includes more than 6,000 municipal policemen, in which they asked the government to maintain capital punishment in Canada and institute a special compensation fund to help the dependents of murder victims.
As to the amendment which was before us earlier, regarding a five-year trial period during which capital punishment would be abolished, I must say that it resembles strangely

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
a suggestion made last year by a Labour member of parliament in Great Britain, Mr. Sydney Silverman who, when lecturing in Canada on a tour at the invitation of a member of the N.D.P. advocated that solution as a substitute or an alternative to the present legislation.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote for the retention of capital punishment, not because I consider that this is a legislation of revenge and prevarication, but because I know that it is the only one we have, at this time, to protect our society against potential criminals and murderers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common with all other members of this house I have been giving the matter which is before us this evening a very great deal of serious thought. I have noticed from the speeches to which I have listened and the comments of my colleagues in the House of Commons that everybody has been giving the subject deep and earnest consideration. Personally, I have tried to weigh the relative merits of the arguments which have been made on both sides, arguments which seemed to be so well balanced that one appeared to offset the other, to the extent that it took me some time before I was able to come to a firm decision.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I did come to a decision. The decision to which I came was that I would have to support the abolition of capital punishment. Granted, there are many factors involved and there are some intangibles for which there is no yardstick. Men of good faith and high principles support both sides; and there is no doubt that the sincerity of the one side, regardless which side it is, is equally matched by the sincerity of the other side.
I reached my conclusion for two particular reasons, among many others, and I should like to deal with them very briefly in a few moments. I do not wish to cover ground that has already been well covered by speakers before me, but I should like to say that it is to be expected that the general character of the people of Canada will be reflected in their laws.
These laws are designed not only to protect society but also to encourage the continuance of the principles which have been an abiding source of strength to all people in our nation.
[Mr. Valade.i
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
In the present debate arguments are made both for an against retaining capital punishment. Those who support retaining capital punishment and those who support its abolition are both endeavouring to bring in legislation which will be for the the betterment of Canada. I think there is no doubt about their intentions. However I believe that capital punishment ought to be abolished, if for no other reason than that to some extent it is unenforceable. It seems that it is becoming more and more difficult to enforce laws on the statute books that prescribe capital punishment. Where hangings are concerned juries seem to be unwilling to bring in verdicts of guilty. Quite often when a man is sentenced to hang, the verdict is changed to one involving penal servitude.
As things are today a man knows when he commits murder that he has an excellent chance, if caught, of not being executed. Therefore what are the advantages of retaining capital punishment? Under circumstances such as these, any deterrent effect capital punishment has is negated by the fact that the sentence to hang is seldom carried out.
I believe that the value of a deterrent depends largely upon the certainty and swiftness with which justice is dispensed. As things are there can be no certainty that capital punishment will be carried out. It is almost certain that when a man is sentenced to hang there will be interminable delays. As I said, juries seem hesitant to bring in verdicts finding accused persons guilty of capital murder, when they know that the convicted man very likely will hang. As a result there are laws on the statute books which are not enforced. That being the case, I maintain that it is better to rewrite the laws than to have them ignored.
On the other hand if the sentence for capital murder were life imprisonment, in my view juries would not be reluctant to bring in verdicts of guilty. There would be a far greater certainty that a murderer would be found guilty and punished if it were realized that the consequences of murder were certain penal servitude for life. I submit that the real deterrent would be the realization by would-be murderers that the law would be enforced, and enforced swiftly.
Another reason why I think hanging should be abolished is the effect that I think legalized killings or executions have upon the public character. When I talk of this I realize that I am talking of something about which it is impossible to quote statistics. It must be a
April 5. 1966

matter of opinion, and it must be something for which there can be only a belief. It cannot be substantiated by fact. I agree with the man who said that whenever a criminal dies on the gallows a little part of the nation dies with him. I believe that an execution by the state has a detrimental effect upon the character of the people. I believe it has a detrimantal effect on both the state and the people. Also, I believe every time a man is hanged, the dragon's teeth for future crime are sow n. I believe by the very means by which we seek to abolish crime we are in fact sowing the seeds of future crime. I believe it is wrong for the state to take upon itself the prerogative to say that it is permissible to kill in the face of the divine command: Thou shalt not kill.
I believe, too, that it is wrong in this modern age, in a country known for its humanities, for its forward looking social thought and conscience, that we should have today as part of our system of justice an instrument of medieval murder which is comparable with the rack and the thumbscrew. I believe it is time that the people of Canada should banish from this land the shadow of the gibbet.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate assuredly not because of the enthusiasm the question under study stirs in me. I do so rather out of a sense of duty, and therefore shall do it fairly rapidly. I have risen simply because I owe it to my electors to let them know where I stand with regard to the abolition or retention of capital punishment. Referring to the correspondence exchanged with my electors, it would seem that the question has not aroused their enthusiasm or interest very much. In fact, I have received only four letters from the people I represent in this house. It is interesting to note that, in one of them, one paragraph reads as follows:
-society must absolutely be protected against this wave of the most revolting crimes.
This shows, Mr. Speaker, that in my electors' opinion, retention of the death penalty reflects not a desire for vengeance but rather a means of giving society the protection it needs.
In addition to those written testimonies which I hold in my hand, I discussed the matter with several of my electors who all
Criminal Code
agreed that society should be properly protected.
Consequently, it will not be news for any of them to learn that I will act according to their wishes and that it will make it a duty to vote in favour of maintaining capital punishment.
During our debate, Mr. Speaker, we have heard the opinions of both sides, the abolitionists as well as the retentionists. I respect those who do not share my opinion and I hope that they, in turn, will respect the opinion of those who do not share theirs.
In the course of our discussion, we had the opportunity of listening to many arguments and, especially of realizing that those who favour the abolition of capital punishment have brushed a very sombre picture of the lot of the murderer who is lead to the gallows. However, I think they forgot to give the complete picture by not referring also to all the inconveniences and harm sustained by those who are related one way or the other to the event, the victim's family.
At this point, I should like to put the following question: What is the result of a murder, when the widow of the man killed must subsequently struggle with all kinds of sad situations? Was there any thought given to the very talented young man, who, for a lack of money to continue his education, must bring it to an abrupt end, thus losing the possible advantages of an enviable and very interesting job which he could have filled in society? And what about the numerous other inconveniences faced by the families of those victims of the deadly bullets of certain people who have lived almost all their lives outside the law.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is our responsibility to take the necessary action to protect society. Have those who are in favour of abolition paid enough attention to the fact that by abolishing the death penalty we would give free rein to the traitors who endanger the very security of our society, of our country? What about the leaders of organized crime, the hired killers and, finally, the habitual criminals who would never miss an opportunity to commit other crimes if they could?
Mr. Speaker, I might have given more attention to that motion if the crime rate today was decreasing instead of increasing. I think it would be a serious mistake at this time, and when the number of crimes is forever increasing, to soften the steps taken to eradicate crime in society.

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
I think it is our duty to keep our eyes open and to give the protection needed. You know as I do that today masked bandits and criminals operate in the remotest regions and commit the most odious crimes in front of people who watch them helplessly. My colleague from Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) told yesterday the story of a tragedy which happened just a few days ago at St. Robert, a very quiet rural community where defenceless people were ill-treated and where crimes which would make your hair stand on end were committed.
Mr. Speaker, I will not say any more but I would like however to be reassured about the steps that will be taken by the government if the abolition of the death penalty is approved tonight and I would also like to know the attitude of the government in case it is maintained.
Personally, I think that with the 1961 amendment it is almost impossible to send an innocent to the gallows. Therefore, I think that by applying the present law, we have the guaranty that everyone gets the proper protection and that, in cases where there is the least doubt, the accused has the possibility of having the facts examined and of claiming his rights fully as provided by the House of Commons and the statutes of Canada.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)

speechtext:
I admit in all sincerity that nobody wants capital punishment to be abolished more than I do, providing there is no one left to deserve it. Let the murderers and gangsters abolish it first, as a retentionist once said.
My colleagues spoke either for or against the death penalty with dignity, conviction and seriousness and they often used arguments or statistics that are open to question. Some indulged in sentimental statements and oratory which, in my opinion, should not have taken up so much of our time in this discussion.
Like other members before me, I should like to give you briefly my opinion and that of the great majority of my constituents on this matter that I find most delicate, one on which everybody has his own idea, while stating that capital punishment is neither a murder nor a vengeance, but a deterrent.
The countries which impose or have imposed it are not murderers; otherwise, you would have to condemn all nations of ancient history and many modern states that have

always insisted on protecting the public interest. Even the Bible refers to it very often, as many pointed out during this debate.
Society, Mr. Speaker, was not formed by accident. It was the will of our Creator that it should exist. It originated in the nature of individual man himself, who is unable to pursue his goal alone and to achieve the full development of his own being without the help of his brethren. Society is not the result of man's will, but of the deepest needs and most imperious aspirations of his nature. It is of divine origin, like our own nature. It received then the necessary means to protect the common weal.
We have to decide if the state should retain or abolish capital punishment as a means which it has by its nature for the greater good of society.
We have been told that capital punishment was justifiable in the days of barbarism, but that in a civilized country it should not exist. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that there will always be, in the various strata of society, a certain category of people in whom the indestructible instincts of cruelty or vengeance will have to be held in check by the salutory fear of death and this applies to us at this time. I believe this. I should like, in particular, to protect those whose duty it is to maintain law and order, and who ask us to retain capital punishment.
Allow me to support most of the arguments of those who preceded me and who advocated retention, although I must say one of the arguments of the retentionists really shook me, and that is the one which accuses society of not having done enough for certain individuals. Society, it would seem, is responsible to some extent for certain murderers. This assertion leads us to ponder on our responsibilities and endeavour to do even better in the future.
I understood the numerous arguments on rehabilitation, but one wonders if we are truly adequately prepared to reform the convicted, materially, morally and spiritually.
Do we have the necessary competence, in quantity and in quality? An army of experts on the rehabilitation of criminals would be needed, and we do not have them. Considering the considerable knowledge required of competent psychologists, surely it is not with guards, more or less sufficiently remunerated, I admit, lacking the required specialized and continuous training, from whom only grade 7 is required and who are in direct contact with the criminals that we can, in spite of
April 5. 19G6

their willingness, infuse what it would take into the convicts.
We must also take into consideration the surroundings in which the prisoners live. They will try more readily to find means to escape and to learn new tricks than to mend their ways. Assuredly, many social and penal reforms should be made; we have made a start, but are we ready to give all these unfortunate people the help they really need?
When we are ready, we will be in a better position to consider abolition of capital punishment, because retention must not be an everlasting and absolute decision.
Mr. Speaker, even though abolitionists were perhaps better prepared for this debate through publicity, I am convinced that we must retain the death penalty at present.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to be as brief as possible and I should like to concentrate on society and its responsibilities. I do not want to repeat what other members have said for or against capital punishment, but simply to point out the responsibilities of our society concerning this vile crime deserving the sentence of death.
Mr. Speaker, the authorities have the right and the duty to punish the bad and reward the good. God Himself does it in this world and in the next. As all power comes from God, the authorities should imitate God: they should punish evil while tempering justice with mercy. Parents themselves, whose authority comes from heaven, have the right to punish and to reward; so have those to whom they entrust the education of children; so has the Church through its spiritual punishments; so has all true authority in this world.
The Ten Commandments of God, and especially one such as "Thou shalt not kill", apply to every human being, for each will be judged according to his virtues and his sins, his merits and demerits. The commandments cannot apply to society, for theft, murder, adultery, lying and so on, are sins and crimes committed by individuals, not by society. Society, through the authority of its legitimate leaders, has the right and the duty to protect its individual members and to punish those who harm them. If the 5th commandment of God forbids a man or those close to the victim of a murder to kill for motives of justice or revenge, because a man is not in himself an authority, society, which has the authority, must intervene and punish if necessary. In wartime, society kills, destroys,
Criminal Code
lies, cheats and violates almost all the commandments and it must not justify itself in the same way as the individual alone or a particular soul. Those who cannot make these distinctions can only live in confusion and make anarchic judgments.
The main arguments of abolitionists are based on emotionalism, sophism, the weakening of the authority required to maintain order, the contradiction of God's commandments, materialism and more often than not, atheism. They are based on a distorted psychology tending to abolish the notion of sin, of personal responsibility, and to find society guilty of all sins and crimes of individuals considered as victims of that society. And since criminals, through this reasoning, become the victims of society, it is felt that those poor victims must be spared, looked after, coddled and even pampered. Is this not topsy-turvydom, the negation of divine rights and authority, of the rights of society to punish evil and protect us from it?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, our society also has responsibilities. It is entrusted with heavy responsibilities and great duties. The strongest, the richest and the shrewdest overwhelm the weak. It is the law of the jungle at its most ferocious, and it can only foster inequalities.
This is being felt in all classes of society. How many middle class or professional people are compelled to compromise with their conscience in order to live according to their rank and their class? Many of us would be amazed if they could scrutinize consciences and realize the disorder created by our antisocial and anti-human economic system.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Our economic system has caused more casualties than the most devastating wars for the last hundred years. We have a great many families who have lived like animals, in hovels, without medical care, without education, without the bare necessities, disinherited, robbed, dispossessed and thrown into the streets by the barbaric, heartless, slanderous system of usury supported by those who are or were responsible for the commonweal; those who protect such a system are guilty of greater crimes than those who have had the misfortune to commit an offence.
Mr. Speaker, several members have reiterated in this house that taking someone's life was forbidden, because life is a gift of God and only He can take it away.

April 5. 1966
Criminal Code
Let us also recall, Mr. Speaker, that God said: "All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword".
This is my answer to these gentlemen: Why then do some men take it upon themselves to organize national or international slaughters? If it is a criminal act to take someone's life, how criminal then are those who have eliminated thousands of human beings under the guise of defending Christendom, Civilization, Democracy, or the Homeland? If so many lives could be destroyed to save various countries, to protect them against aggression, it should also be permitted to sentence to death a habitual criminal for the protection of society. I think it is our duty to do so. But here again, a great number of those crimes are due to our anti-Christian, anti-moral and anti-humanitarian system.
I agree with the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) that we should put more Christianity in our schools, in our institutions, in our lives. Mr. Speaker, the day we have in our legislatures, men who do not fear what people say and who have taken the undertaking to act according to justice as revealed by God and to legislate so that justice prevails in Canada and in modern America, they can once more reveal to the nation the secret of permanent freedom and justice and show the world the great ways of a durable peace.
To that end, we must reinforce our army and increase its units; but we must above all organize another sort of army, an army of devoted revolutionaries, composed of men and women who will wage an all-out war on injustice and corruption because they will not be afraid of having their lives exposed, of men and women who do not protect the corruption of others, of men and women who do not despise problems, of men and women who will face problems with firmness instead of avoiding them, of men and women who will strictly apply the principles of honesty, purity and unselfishness in their daily life. We must not only seek to contain and check the criminal world, but we must change it, and, to that end, we must believe in the Lord's Prayer: "Thy will be done on earth as it is in Heaven."
If God's will is done on earth by men who listen to him and obey him, surely remedial measures can be taken at the political, economic and social levels so as to ensure education and change the environment.
All this is urgent, but it will take more than laws to face up to hate, dispel fear, destroy envy and put an end to colour, race

and environment selfishness, which are the sources of our divisions.
Mr. Speaker, we have remained stunted in the moral and spiritual fields; we have to live with a civilization craving for pills and excitement, where people while away boredom by looking at sex films or films of violence, and taking pep pills or sleeping pills, or ulcer pills. Often we cannot bring unity in our homes, in industry or in our country, to say nothing of our incapacity to do anything in a world torn up by fear, envy and hate.
Nowadays, a nation should not be afraid to stand up and say what is right and what is wrong. If we uphold what is right, as God shows it to us, in domestic or foreign affairs, in our private life as well as in our national life, then our private life and our national life will both be spent for the eternal happiness of each and every one of us.
Mr. Speaker, capital punishment is the only penalty that fits the seriousness of the crime of murder. The punishment imposed for a serious crime should be commensurate with the horror it arouses in most people; in the final analysis, punishment is justified because it emphatically constitutes condemnation of a crime by the community.
From this point of view, some murders deserve the ultimate sentence, that of death, provided that justice be the same for all and that the influential, the upstarts and the rich share the same fate.
Mr. Speaker, the death penalty is a just punishment for the greatest crime of all and may alone atone for an unforgiveable crime.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, our society has great responsibilities. Before making a decision which will greatly affect society, its future and the future of crime in society, I would like each member to ponder the strongest arguments. I think that the strongest argument is to have recourse to punishment of the Divine Providence, to put the question in the hands of Providence.
And on these words, I close saying that I shall vote against the abolition of capital punishment. I shall also vote against the proposed amendment, which recommends capital punishment only when policemen or prison guards have been murdered for, in my opinion, the members of society must be protected and respected as much as any policeman. I know that they, whose duty it is to maintain order in society, are more exposed than the others, but that is no reason to protect only them. All citizens must be protected, equally and justly. Justice must be
April S, 1966

done, it must triumph according to natural law and divine law.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not planned to take part whatsoever in this debate from the opening day of the five now devoted to this subject until the vote tonight, but in view of some circumstances which developed a few days ago I now wish to make plain the position of those of us who are called retentionists, of whom there are a large number in this house.
The government house leader introduced a motion some time ago which required the unanimous consent of the house, to set aside government business for three days in order that we might discuss a private member's resolution introduced in the names of four individual members of this house. This motion required unanimous consent. While it called for the abolition of the death penalty the retentionists in the house did not raise any objection to it, and we had three days' discussion on the question.
Upon the conclusion of the three days of debate, which was all that the abolilionists asked for, an objection was raised to continuing the debate because government business was being set aside and the national work of the country was being delayed and held up. The retentionists considered that there was very important government work to be done. As a result of the objection raised by the retentionists, and I am using that word in its plural form, we were able to pass the supplementary estimates for the year ending March 31, 1966 during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1966.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Then efforts were made to bring back into the discussion stage this question of the abolition of capital punishment. Unanimous consent was again required from the members of the house, including the retentionists of whom there are a large number. The retentionists are very, very anxious to have brought on to the floor of this house and discussed a private members' notice of motion which stands in my name. This notice of motion is No. 22 and can be found on page 26 of today's Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day. It was introduced on January 20, two days after the house assembled, because the retentionists in this house are thinking of the victims of murderers more than they are thinking of the criminal element who perform the murders.
Criminal Code
This resolution which stands in my name, but was introduced on behalf of all retentionists in the house, was drawn up properly by the senior law officers of the crown. You will find the wording as follows:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should consider the expediency of introducing legislation for the creation of a Criminal Injuries Compensation Board to hear the pleas of persons who have suffered permanent injury or disability as the victims of crime and award compensation to such persons or their dependents as would seem fair in the circumstances, and wherever possible to do so, to impose payment of compensation by criminals to those they have injured.
This resolution could be based on any one of a large number of cases, but I am thinking in particular of a murder that occurred in the area of Toronto in which I live. A little seven-year old girl was murdered by a man who was, of course, later judged insane. He was considered sane right up to the time of the murder, although he was then 24 years of age. You realize, of course, that in the first 24 years of his life they could not tell whether he was insane or not, but the moment he committed a murder he was judged insane immediately.
In other words, they take one half hour of his life, as compared with the 24 years he had lived and was considered sane, and find him to be insane. The little girl was in our Sunday school and when she was murdered, and foully murdered, a fund was started in the section of Toronto in which I reside and go to church. I go to church in the riding of High Park although I live in the riding of York-Humber. A fair collection was taken on behalf of the little child. The amount collected paid for the funeral, the funeral plot and left some money over for the distraught mother, her husband and the little girl's brothers and sisters. But once that little sum of money, which had been contributed by Christians and other people of compassionate minds and hearts, was expended, that was the end of it.
I was a newspaper reporter for eight years, although I was in the newspaper business for a total of 40 years. During the time I was a newspaper reporter I covered several murder trials and had the bitter experience more than once of having to interview the families of murder victims. In these cases I never had anything to comment except unfavourably, because of what results from the action of murderers.
We retentionists believe that the federal government should establish a financial fund that would make payments regularly to the

April 5. 1966
Criminal Code
families of victims of murder and other criminal acts. This resolution was introduced on January 20 and I made a personal plea to certain ministers that it be brought on the floor of the house before the resolution for the abolition of capital punishment was introduced. I received absolutely no answer.
I and the retentionists in this house have more interest in the victims of murderers than we have in the murderers themselves. If a person is flying in a Trans-Canada Air Lines plane and the plane crashes, such as occurred at Ste Therese, Quebec, and your loved ones are killed, you can collect from T.C.A., which I suppose you might say is the government. Some lawyer will get up and tell me it is not the government, that this is a crown corporation and is not the government at all. But we pay the deficits.
You collect from the government if you lose a loved one through an accident on-I said Trans-Canada Air Lines but for the benefit of those who want it I will say Air Canada. You knew what I meant when I said Trans-Canada Air Lines, anyway. If you are in the province of Ontario, and I cannot speak of the other eight as well, and a man-

speechtext: The other eight? There are nine.
