speechtext:
-driving a motor car runs into you or your loved ones and someone is killed, if you cannot collect cash from the person who caused the collision and the death in your family you can institute an action and collect compensation from the unsatisfied judgments fund administered by the Ontario government through the Department of Highways. I refer to a death occasioned by an accident involving motorcars. Or you might be walking up the street in your own municipality and trip over a broken sidewalk, fall very heavily on the ground, fracture your skull and die within a couple of hours or days. Then the family sues the municipality and receives compensation for the death in the family. But if someone in your family is murdered by a criminal, we turn all the strength of the crown in behind the criminal to see that he gets three meals a day, has a warm bed, is looked after properly and is given a psychiatric examination. What about the victim? The attitude is: The victim is dead; skip it.
I say that if we can collect through accidents in an Air Canada plane and from the government behind Air Canada, if we can collect from the government of the provinces

because of a motorcar accident and our loved ones are killed or die as a result of the accident, if we can collect from the municipalities if we should fall or trip due to some faulty work in the municipality, the families of victims of murderers and other criminal acts should also be compensated by the state, because they did not bring the situation on themselves.
When I asked the law officers of the crown, on behalf of the retentionists, if they would prepare this resolution, I said to the law officers that I wanted it drawn up on the basis that the families of victims of murderers should be able to collect in a cash way, if not from the criminal-whom the abolitionists are everlastingly telling us are poor, poor, poor-then from the government. According to the abolitionists the rich are never murderers; it seems that only the poor are murderers. They never point out that 80 per cent of the world's population are poor, so of course 80 per cent of the murderers will be poor. They just refer to the large number of murderers who are poor.
If the family of the victim cannot collect from the murderer or the murderer's family, surely they are as entitled to collect from the state as the family of a person who is killed in an Air Canada plane, on the highways of a province or due to negligence on the part of a municipality.
We retentionists gave unanimous consent, although we could have withheld it, to have the discussion of this resolution against capital punishment resumed for a fourth and a fifth day. The newspapers, those men and women who sit a long way from us and can read our minds as though they were an open book-I noticed this comment in some of the mass media-said that pressure was going to be applied here, pressure was going to be applied there, the steam-roller was going to roll and the whips were going to crack. Let me say in all fairness to the gentlemen who have conducted this debate that there has been no pressure at any time, of any kind, applied to any retentionist. There has not even been any conversation with any retentionist. This debate has been conducted properly and in a high-minded way, I believe, by the ladies and gentlemen who compose the House of Commons. But the retentionists went along with unanimous consent because they wanted me to present this argument at this time.
April 5, 1966



[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We have co-operated. We granted unanimous consent for the first three days. We granted unanimous consent for the fourth and the fifth day. We granted unanimous consent so the leader of the Conservative Party was able to continue beyond his 20 minutes. We granted unanimous consent so that the leader of the New Democratic party was able to continue beyond his 20 minutes, although we knew both were abolitionists. We granted unanimous consent for the continuation of the debate from ten o'clock to 11.30 last night. We granted unanimous consent for no division to be taken during that period and for the day's adjournment proceedings to be deferred. We retentionists have granted unanimous consent on about ten different occasions in the last two weeks to aid those people who want to mollycoddle the criminal element of Canada by reducing the severity of the punishment stated in the Criminal Code of Canada. At this time we would like the house leader of the government, and the cabinet, to please allow the retentionists one day in which government business will be cleared away so that we can discuss this resolution No. 22 calling for compensation to the families and victims of criminal acts.
When the law officers of the crown were preparing this resolution, they said to us: You do not want this resolution prepared simply as though all the victims were murdered. They remarked: We know your heart and we know your mind on this point. If a girl were being attacked by, let me say, an ape, a word synonymous with this type of man, and she cried out, perhaps as a result of having vitriolic acid thrown in her face to blind her, and gentlemen came rushing to her aid while the ape disappeared, that girl might be left blinded for life, although she had not been murdered. These officers of the crown said that they had prepared this resolution to cover a case like that, also, where a person has been attacked by a criminal and has suffered permanent injury, the family has suffered damages and compensation should be made available to that family.
Now, of course, the situation is much worse in a case where the breadwinner is murdered and a widow may be left with children to look after. What compensation does the state provide? The state provides none. The retentionists are asked, out of their Christian hearts and compassionate minds, to contribute to a fund for the relief of those families 23033-247
Criminal Code
where the breadwinner has been murdered. I say that before we start easing the severity of punishment on murderers, we should give consideration to looking after the families of the victims, not only of murderous attacks but of other criminal attacks.
On behalf of the retentionists in the House of Commons, I ask that the government-not in the distant future, not in due course and after consideration, not after the Easter vacation or when the matter has been given every possible consideration or an inquiry has been made by the justice department-grant the retentionists a day, right away. We retentionists have granted unanimous consent regularly during the past two weeks. The government has set government business aside. They have even set aside the discussion of the budget.
We simply ask for one day. We do not think that is too much, considering that we have given unanimous consent for a five-day discussion for those who want to aid and abet the criminal population. We now want one day so that we can direct the cabinet's attention to the question of arranging for compensation for those families who may have lost their breadwinner, may have lost the mother of children, may have lost a child in his teens whom they have raised at great expense and was just coming to be a financial satisfaction to his parents, only to be done away with by a murderer. A family may have lost a dearly beloved baby by a murderous attack. What has the state cared up to this moment? It has done nothing: The victim is dead, so let the dead bury their dead. It says, in effect: let us find the murderer, we will make a gentleman out of him by buying some more psychiatric couches, putting him in prison for life and feeding him well. The retentionists ask for a little attention to the families of the victims.
I do not intend to comment further on this debate, except to say that I am opposed to the amendment. I am opposed to the main motion. The man or woman does not live who can tell me that the persons set out in this amendment, a police officer, prison guard, constable, sheriff, deputy sheriff, sheriff's officer or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, is of more value to me than my wife or any one of my three daughters.
I believe that the death sentence is a deterrent. The abolitionists believe that the death sentence is a deterrent or they would not be introducing an amendment such as this which would prevent the murder of a

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
police officer or prison guard by holding up the tear of the noose to those who might murder them.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because I have
strong feelings about the question of law enforcement in general, because I have strong feelings about respect for the law, because I have strong feelings in connection with the loyalty and support that the citizens of any country should give to the officers charged with law enforcement within the coniines of that country, I feel I should have something to say on the resolution before the house. Now, in order to refresh our minds, I should like to read the resolution itself. I quote:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Criminal Code for the purposes of
(a)	abolishing the death penalty in respect of all offences under that act;
I particularly draw to the attention of the house the words, "all offences". I continue to quote:
(b)	substituting a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment in those cases where the death penalty is now mandatory; and
(c)	providing that no person upon whom a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment is imposed shall be released from imprisonment without the prior approval of the governor in council.
I find myself looking at the meaning of the word "expedient". I realize that we in this house frequently use and understand the meaning of the word "expedient". However, this is not an ordinary resolution. This is a resolution that is going to change something which affects many people, something upon which we all have very strong views. I am one who has been impressed by the arguments that have been advanced. Some of these arguments have been temperate while others have been quite emotional. Nevertheless these arguments have been advanced, I feel, by people who feel strongly about this subject.
I looked up the meaning of the word "expedient". I find that the Oxford dictionary gives the following meanings for the word "expedient": (1) advantageous; (2) suitable; (3) politic rather than just. So far as advantageous is concerned, in this day of increasing violence everyone will ask what possible advantage could there be by removing a possible deterrent to murder.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
With regard to the second meaning, that is, suitable, what makes a time when respect for

human life is becoming less with each passing day a suitable time to be taking away a possible deterrent to the murder of the innocent? Then, we come to the last meaning, politic rather than just. Surely we, as members of this house, are not so much concerned with the letters and protests received from those who I feel, quite inadvertently, would appear to favour the attacker rather than the victim. I think we have to legislate to protect society to the greatest possible degree. This becomes our duty. I contend that in a period of frightening increase in crime in Canada it is neither advantageous, suitable nor politic to remove from our statute books the death penalty, especially in the case of certain heinous crimes.
I feel that in debating this question we are putting the cart before the horse, as was said this afternoon by another speaker. I feel we should be debating and diligently seeking ways and means to control the criminal elements in our society and to get rid of the international crime rings, which we are told are even now entrenching themselves in our country. No doubt these people are following this present debate with more than average interest.
I feel that we should be debating and seeking ways and means of strengthening the hand of our law enforcement officers rather than placing their lives in further jeopardy. I believe they deserve to be fully supported in their difficult job of protection, and that never should undue pressure be brought to bear upon them.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is not a question of what we might be debating here; it is what we are debating. What we are debating is simply whether it is expedient to abolish the death penalty and to replace it with life imprisonment, subject to certain reservations. I cannot subscribe to the general idea that there is a great advantage in bringing about such a change. I do not believe that such a change as this should be made in the statutes of this country merely upon a majority vote. I believe there should be at least a two thirds majority before any legislation such as envisaged by this resolution is passed.
I feel that we have to pay some attention to our law enforcement officers. We have ample evidence that law enforcement officers in practically every province of the country have expressed the opinion that the abolition of the death penalty is not in the interests of justice. Provincial attorneys general, judges
April 5, 1S66

and many people who have dealt with criminals consider that the death penalty is a definite deterrent.
This is not the first time that this subject has come before the house. But I believe that this is the first time the government of the day has asked the house for a yes or no decision in the matter. I believe that resolutions of this nature have been talked out previously, as we say here, but this government has asked us for a decision. I presume that an amendment to the Criminal Code will follow such decision, if favourable. However, it seems to me that the whole question is too important for it to be confined to the judgment of just a few people. I feel the question should be carefully examined by an impartial tribunal in the light of existing circumstances and amendments made in 1961.
Having mentioned the amendments of 1961 let me immediately recall what must be obvious to everybody. These amendments have been in operation now for less than five years. After a limited time of operation we now have presented to us a resolution which pretty well does away with the flexibility, if you like, of the amendments made in 1961. We have a resolution which seeks to change the law, one which expresses the view that the death penalty should be abolished.
The fact that this resolution is before us today suggests that something must have been lacking in the amendments made in 1961. Mr. Speaker, I do not subscribe to that general idea. I do not believe that there is anything very much lacking in the amendments of 1961. Therefore, as we come nearer to the time to vote on this resolution, why do we not look at the amendments to see what they embody?
In my opinion these amendments gave very definite and most reasonable protection to a person accused of murder, short of total abolition of the death penalty. Capital murder, as compared with non-capital murder, is clearly defined. According to the white paper on capital punishment which was prepared by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) in June of 1965, persons under 18 are exempted from capital charges. Up to September 1961 any person convicted of murder was sentenced to death. From that time on, owing to the distinction made between capital and non-capital murder, which was clearly defined, only those convicted of murders which had been deliberately planned or committed in crimes of violence by the direct
Criminal Code
intervention or counselling of the accused, were sentenced to death. The death penalty was also imposed for the murder of a police officer or a prison guard acting in the course of duty and which resulted from such direct intervention or counselling. Additional information regarding the charge of capital murder and the charge of non-capital murder can be found at pages 66, 67 and 68 of the book which I hold in my hand.
The present law concerning a person convicted of the charge of capital murder should be well known. But I sometimes wonder whether it is realized that the decision whether a charge of capital murder or noncapital murder is laid is made by the local prosecutor after consultation with the Attorney General of the province in which the crime is committed. Surely if there is any doubt in the mind of the Attorney General or the chief law officer of the crown in any province, the accused will be charged with the lesser offence of the two, which would be non-capital murder, and this is a protective feature.
Since 1961 an accused person is arraigned on a charge of capital murder only if the Attorney General or crown attorney is satisfied that that is the proper charge to be laid. From there on the procedure is well known by all. Twelve jurors are sworn before the judge and they hear the evidence. The jury determines questions of fact, the judge determines questions of law. At the conclusion of the cases for the prosecution and the defence the jury decides upon the guilt of the accused. Still another safeguard is the fact that the judge asks the jury whether there is any recommendation for mercy, and such recommendation, generally speaking, brings a commutation.
With the above facts in mind, it seems to me that those who argue that an innocent person may suffer the death penalty are talking about something most unlikely to happen in light of the amendments of 1961. The fact must also be faced-and I do not say this critically-that for the past three years the present government has commuted every death sentence. Commutations have become ordinary rather than extraordinary. I have always felt that every time there was a commutation there was a feeling of rejoicing among criminals.
It has been argued that the death penalty is not a deterrent to the crime of murder. I submit it is, and I base that submission on the fact that nothing is dearer than life itself.

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
The old saying that "while there's life there's hope" applies. There is another old expression to the effect that were it not for fear of the law, man would commit murder. These old expressions are probably cliches and trite, but nevertheless there is usually an element of wisdom in them.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Before leaving the subject of the 1961 amendments, I believe it is proper for me to say that a five-year trial period is not long enough. Before the present resolution was presented to us there should have been an examination made of the results under the amendments. Has experience indicated an improvement as compared with the situation which existed prior to 1961? That is one of the questions to be asked. Should the amendments be given a longer period of time in order to determine whether they are sufficient or insufficient?
One of my reasons for voting against the resolution before us is that the 1961 amendments have not had sufficient time to demonstrate their effectiveness or otherwise. I once asked a distinguished judge of the Supreme Court of Ontario his opinion on the abolition of the death penalty. I wish I could quote his reply. He referred to instance after instance of killers whose sentences had been commuted to life imprisonment, who were later released and sent out into society to strike again. One such man killed three times before he was finally condemned. The judge said: "My experience shows that there are people who are definitely killers."
In our determination to do what is best I believe we should be very much influenced by what is good for the defence of society. We must act in the public interest. The protection of law abiding citizens who still make up the vast majority of the people who sent us here for that purpose, must be put first. I have no hesitation in saying that I believe it is the duty of all of us to do all in our power for the protection of the people who have entrusted to us that duty that responsibility.
We know that there are organized gangs of criminals whose business is murder. Dare we say to these criminals these words; "Come to Canada where we have abolished the death penalty. It will be easier for you there to kill. In Canada there is no crime, no matter how vicious or often repeated, that is punishable by death. And what does life imprisonment, so called, amount to these days? Perhaps ten

years and you are free again, the way things are going today."
Do we want to take the responsibility of having said that to any organized criminals? I, personally, am not willing to take that responsibility. Sometimes I think that there is altogether too much attention-and this has been mentioned by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan)-paid by well in-tentioned people to the criminal who has committed murder, and too little attention paid to his victim. How terrible the experience of the victim must have been. What an agonizing ordeal the victim must have gone through. Put yourselves in the place of such a victim. It might be a small child; more often it is an old person living alone. It could be a taxi driver sitting unprotected on the front seat of his automobile. It could be a storekeeper with a cash register, and with something worth stealing. The victim could be a police officer on duty or someone who in the carrying out of community service must be out alone at night. The victims might be even whole families said to be rich, as in the case so minutely described in Truman Capote's much talked about book, "In Cold Blood". The book brings out the fact that the plan for killing a man and wife and two children was made while the two criminals were in the penitentiary. They heard that the people lived in a somewhat isolated place; that they were well to do people. The motive was robbery. A very cold-blooded murder was planned, carried out, and only a very small sum of money realized. My reason for going into some detail about this incident is simply to emphasize that we must be governed by our desire to protect the innocent and defenceless people at all times. That is my opinion. We may differ on how best to do this, but let us not differ in our concern for those who need protection. Let us not differ in the need to reduce crime and violence as much as possible.
An interesting sidelight on the criminal character is brought out in this best seller, "In Cold Blood". It is that the two killers so minutely described in the book would swerve their car and speed up in order to kill a dog on the road. Senator McGrand, organizer and first president of the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies said: "Where there is no respect for life itself, there is no real respect for human life". The victims of a killer have no judge or jury of 12 to say they should not die. They have no body of legislators such as are assembled today in the Canadian House
April 5, 1966

of Commons to argue that they should not die. They die, and that is the end of it.
We have societies for the rehabilitation of the criminal. More power to them; they are needed. But I have yet to hear of societies devoted to helping the widow and children of a murdered man. I wonder why public sympathy seems to be so misplaced. Is it because the public has become so accustomed to see crimes of violence night after night on television, that many people now take death by violence as something which happens all the time, or as mere play acting? Can you not hear the words: "It is not real; it is just a show".
Unfortunately the play frequently turns to grim reality. I am convinced that many crimes, especially those committed by juveniles and immature adults, are brought about by what these people have seen on television. Violence on television is glamourized. You hear people saying: "Television is a wonderful thing". Yet, who makes a serious attempt to turn this wonderful modern medium into a means for education, for better living, rather than what it seems to be today, which is a means of education for delinquency and crime? I wonder if something ought not to be done-[DOT]

speechtext:
Thank you. An hon. member asks how long I shall be. I say, perhaps three or four minutes.
In voting on this resolution, I consider that I have no choice. I should like however to support legislation which will contribute to the protection of society. I believe I should repeat these words: Our responsibility is the protection of our people, who in many cases are helpless women and children against whom at any time crimes may be committed.
I say that it is clearly the duty of members of parliament to support and enact laws, and to vote money for the protection of those who
Criminal Code
have entrusted to us that duty and responsibility, and that great honour. Therefore, my approach to the question of the treatment of a person who has committed a crime classed as capital murder is entirely from the standpoint of what is the best course to follow in order to legislate a maximum deterrent.
It has been argued that many nations have discontinued capital punishment. That is correct. Many have gone back to it. Great Britain has once more abolished the death penalty. It has been referred to in this debate that in the year 1965 there was a most alarming increase in the murder rate. The Daily Express had the figures and they are here, but as the house has been good enough to allow me to finish my remarks, I shall not go into them. However, there was an alarming increase in 1965 as compared with 1964. I know it may be argued that the next year the rate may be down. However, the proposition advanced is not one-sided.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I was impressed by many speeches, especially that this afternoon by the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Wadds). I was also impressed by the speech made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) a week or so ago. He asked questions. So far I have not heard those questions answered. These were questions that were troubling him and they are troubling me too. He wanted to know what life imprisonment meant. No one has taken the trouble to define it.
He referred to organized murder syndicates that exist in large centres both in the United States and Canada, syndicates made up of people willing to murder other people for money-blood money. No one has said anything about that. In completely renouncing the death penalty do we render their business easier to carry on? My hon. friend from Bow River also raised this question: Do we make life safer and more secure for law abiding citizens when we mollycoddle criminals?
It is my considered judgment that the amendments made to the Criminal Code in 1961 should be given a longer testing period. They are a far more lenient approach to the whole problem of the treatment of a murderer than existed previously. Why do we want to substitute something else after less than five years experience of something which was based on a more lenient approach to criminals? I fail to understand that.
I cannot support the resolution as presently presented. I favour retention of tin death

April 5, 1966
Criminal Code
penalty for certain crimes such as premeditated murder, treason, murder of a policeman or prison guard, and for repeaters. My basic approach to the question is that I am convinced it would be most unwise to make a decision on what is really only part of the problem of the treatment which the state should inflict upon a citizen who has taken the law into his own hands and committed the crime of murder. I use the word treatment rather than punishment because I am sure in my own mind that no one today connects the death penalty with punishment for a crime. The removal of danger from innocent people is what the law was designed to accomplish.
When I vote on this resolution I am going to be influenced by the following: Do 1 vote to protect innocent and law abiding citizens from death by violence, or do I vote to be more lenient with the criminal who has deliberately planned violent death and has been convicted of the same after due deliberation? So far as I am concerned I shall vote to protect the law abiding citizens, and on this basis shall vote against the resolution as presently constituted.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of being able to express myself this evening because initially-and I am going back about 18 months-I was quoted as being a retentionist and against the abolition of the death penalty. Subsequently I was quoted as favouring the abolition of the death penalty. I did not come to this opinion without some study. My basic reading was on the value of the death penalty as a deterrent, and as I read the authorities on the deterrent value I wondered whether or not I was just emotionally wound up in this thing, and therefore I swung toward the abolitionist side.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
That is all right, Mr. Speaker. I represent the riding of Wentworth. There are 56,000 people who vote there and I do not believe they are all wrong; and when I returned to my riding and spoke to them I found the majority do want retention of the penalty. I was sure then that they were not all emotionally involved, that there had to be an idea behind it and, if this was the case,
(Mr. Flemming.]
maybe I had approached the subject from the wrong point of view, namely whether or not the death penalty was a deterrent.
The more I looked at it the more I realized that this probably was an irrelevant argument. Nevertheless, as I heard many hon. members talk about the subject I started to look at figures, and in this connection I quote from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics report, catalogue No. 85209, at page 11.
There I see that murders reported to the D.B.S. in 1956 ranged about one in every 10,000, and homicide deaths resulting therefrom were 1.2 in every 10,000. This was a pretty consistent figure. It was .9 in 1955, 1.0 in 1956, .9 in 1957 and 1.1 in 1958. The corresponding homicidal deaths in those years were 1.2, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2 and 1.4 in 1958.
Then in 1961 we introduced the definition of capital and non-capital murder, and we had wholesale commuting of the death penalty through 1962, 1963 and 1964. Murders reported to the D.B.S. in those years were 1.4, 1.4, and 1.4 per 10,000, and homicidal deaths resulting therefrom were 1.6, 1.5, 1.5,-about a 40 per cent increase on the average. Whether wholesale commuting started the trend I do not know, but it certainly caused me to wonder whether or not I should re-examine the situation.
From the figures it appeared that either the deterrent value was not there or else the Canadian people were becoming more lawless in their outlook toward crimes of violence, and if this is the case then I can only put forward something of my own thinking. I am not going to dwell on the evolution of capital punishment. We have heard many abolitionists talk about the death penalty for nickel and dime crimes. This is no longer the case and I am very glad it is not. However we have refined the death penalty down to the point where it is only applicable for premeditated murder, treason, and crimes of violence. I do not believe that the death penalty is a neurosis of our judicial system. I feel it has been refined to the point where it is an absolute necessity.
Out last amendment to the Criminal Code in 1961 divided murder into two classes, capital and non-capital, and I do not believe we have had a true test of the fairness or the efficiency of this law. It is the erosion of this rule of law that frightens me, and I shall return to this later.
Today the death penalty stands as the supreme punishment for those who defy our way of life and prefer to live with violence
April 5, 1966

and mayhem. It is not used basically as a deterrent today, it is not used as revenge: It is used as the basis of the security in which our people live.
It has amazed me how many people have told me, "I do not really know why I want the death penalty retained, but I do know that if it is abolished it is a weakening of my rights. It is a weakening of the protection I have against those people who do not want to live within the laws we have designed for ourselves."
It is all very well for the abolitionists to stand up and plead for the dignity of life and the salvation of a convicted killer, but I am not sure that John Doe, citizen, is ready to accept the return of these killers into society, or even that he wants the responsibility of looking after them while they are incarcerated.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I also have sat here for three or four days listening to this debate and I always have felt as I sat here with my colleagues-and I am speaking of colleagues on all sides of house-that we represent 18 million Canadians; these are the Canadians who look to us and ask us to decide on laws for their protection and for their welfare. I do not believe we are doing that when we are allowing the possibility, or probability, of some men who cannot live within our laws being turned back into society. Nobody has any guarantee he is going to be able to live there within the law, but everybody is afraid that he will take a life again or will again destroy.
Earlier I mentioned an erosion of the rule of law. I believe throughout the world today our legislatures are taking away the rights of the individual. They are taking away these rights in different ways, so that in many of the matters which are a part of their way of life, people are deprived of basic rights which would have been protected by adherence to the rule of law.
Akin to this there also is something which has worried me and given me great concern; that is, the general lack of discipline we have among us and a disregard for any authority. I think a good example of this is a report of picketing in Oshawa not very long ago. This report is to the effect that there were so-called picketers who had ignored a court injunction and who had torn up this injunction after it had been read by the sheriff. What makes it even more frightening today is
Criminal Code
that on that picket line were prominent people whom we like to think of as our leaders; one was Mr. C. H. Millard, one of the persons we imported as a trustee of the S.I.U.; another was the leader of the New Democratic party in the province of Ontario.
Another incident which has given me some concern-and it was mentioned earlier this afternoon-was the comment of one of our judges in Ontario to the effect that it was a waste of time to pursue a capital murder charge, and he went to the lesser one of non-capital murder.
This outbreak may have been poorly timed. Nevertheless to me, and I am sure to many people who read those headlines, it was indicative of the disregard in which law is held today through the ill use of executive power. Instead of abolishing the death penalty at this time, I say it is better that we return to the proper use of capital and noncapital legislation, with some hope that, if we here in the house give a mandate, the executive branch will re-examine the royal prerogative and use it, not as a salve to their conscience, if this is what they have been doing, or as a stop-gap pending new legislation, if this is what they have been doing, but rather use it in the circumstances for which it was designed-extraordinary circumstances with a plea for clemency from judge or jury, or both.
In closing I might suggest to the abolitionist who says there are two types of law, one for the rich and one for the poor, that it is a deplorable situation, but it should not be allowed to influence the erosion of law. It could be argued that the rich should be deprived of the right to legal representation because the poor cannot afford it. This is a problem which could well be taken in hand by a strong and energetic law society, if it feels that it has failed to provide good representation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the death penalty is archaic; I do not think it is useless, although I might say that possibly the way we administer it is archaic. If we are going to make a change, then let us not abolish the death penalty but rather change the way we administer it.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT REGARDING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
As everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, we now are in the dying minutes of what has been a long, interesting and thoughtful debate. In the few minutes

April 5. 1986
Criminal Code
which remain I think it would be impossible for anybody to add anything to what has been said in the way of information. I certainly do not intend to attempt to do so. However as one of the movers of the resolution I did wish to say one or two words about the debate, and if I have the time, I should like to make a brief summary of the position we have been trying to present. I do this, Mr. Speaker, because no matter what the outcome of this debate, I do not think in our own hearts any of us have any doubt with regard to the result which will be achieved here tonight. I believe the earlier vote is symptomatic of what likely will be the result when the main motion is called.
This debate may not have been the greatest debate in parliament, but to me, it certainly is the finest debate in which I have participated since I came to this parliament away back three elections ago in 1962. Some of us who are newer members, Mr. Speaker, at times despair that our parliament ever is able to come to grips with what we think are fundamental problems. We often, or at least I do, feel a sense of frustration in that we never seem to be able to come to grips with the problems which stir us and reach our basic emotions. I do not think we can say that any longer.
I have sat through all the speeches in this debate, because I was one of the sponsors. I think it has served an extremely useful purpose, no matter what the outcome may be. I think it has forced us as members to put aside much of our partisanship and has permitted us to discuss, think about, and deal with matters of life and death and our attitude toward these things and toward all society which we hope to lead and which we endeavour to govern. It has compelled us to think about the criminal as well as the victim; it has made us think about the victim and his relatives; it has made us consider the relatives of the murderer and the stigma which will follow them all the days of their lives.
Many of our members have conducted a refresher course in religion. This too has been interesting. It has forced us in this chamber to look at the whole range of our scale of justice, its treatment of the accused, its injustice to the victim, its failure to curtail crime, its admitted inability to rehabilitate the criminal, and has shown us that we do not even understand the cause of crime much less its solution. For that reason I hope the debate will have served a useful purpose.

I should like to pay tribute to the other co-sponsors of the resolution, throughout the course of the debate, for their co-operation; the co-operation of all of them was unlimited, unprejudiced and of the highest order; it was a great pleasure to work with them.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I want to thank, on behalf of the sponsors, all members in all parts of the house who have participated in this debate for the consideration they have given to the motion and for the manner in which they have treated it. I think all members who have participated- and I have listened to all the speeches-have spoken deeply, sincerely and honestly. Though I may disagree with many-indeed, I anticipate I will disagree with the majority tonight-I hope that nothing I have said or that my supporters have said will be taken by those with whom we differ as implying that they are barbaric, or lacking in mercy, or that their concern for the well-being of the community, the protection of its citizens and the suppression of crime is any less than ours. I say that in all sincerity.
I think, Mr. Speaker, this debate has demonstrated that in all parts of the house our objectives are the same. It is the means to achieve them upon which we differ. All members who have spoken have voiced a concern for dealing with the problems of crime and for deterring the crime of murder. The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) raised the whole problem of compensation. I suspect there would hardly be a dissenting voice in this chamber if a motion of that type were to come forward. Those of us who advocate the abolition of the death penalty have always suggested that we are not mollycoddling the criminal. We hate murder and we hate crime: We have just suggested that the methods we now use to control it are not adequate and are not the only unique deterrents. We have always supported the principle of compensation for victims.
If there is one sad note in this debate it is to me that in the midst of the entire five days we have not heard from three of the top judicial officers in the land. No matter what the outcome of this vote, to me it will always be a source of personal regret that we did not have the benefit of the views and experience of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) or the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell). I feel sorry that in the midst of this debate they have sat mute, in silence, their views, intentions and experiences unregistered.
April 5, 1966

In this debate those of us who support abolition of capital punishment have tried to develop its historical background to point out to the house that we are not really doing any thing new, but that we are merely taking the last step in a long process of evolutionary change. We have accepted the view from the beginning that there is no member of this house who likes hanging, and that all hon. members who wish to retain hanging do so out of a sense of revulsion but of conviction in their minds that it is the only effective deterrent to the crime of murder.
Mr. Speaker, we have disputed this suggestion and we have tried to put on the record the experience of other jurisdictions where hanging has been removed with no appreciable change and with no effect upon the population or upon its safety. We have emphasized our view that the whole question of emotion surrounding hanging inhibits and confuses any sort of systematic attack upon the problems of crime. We have said that the real solution to crime does not lie in this type of penalty, but in greater emphasis upon the strength of our police, their salaries, their training; upon more courts and more adequate methods of detection. I feel that all the emotion which has surrounded the problem of hanging inhibits, deters and restricts us in this very serious goal.
Above all, we have tried to suggest that this whole question should be dealt with in a calm, reasonable and rational way. Indeed it has been a source of surprise to me to sit in the chamber and observe the tremendous emotion that has been generated. I had thought that the point before the house was a very simple and narrow one, as to whether or not we could take the last step and remove hanging as the penalty for capital murder. Instead we have gone very far afield, and great heat and emotion has been generated. This is perhaps inevitable under the circumstances, when we are dealing with a subject that touches people so deeply and upon which they feel so strongly.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, I am only hoping to run out the clock for another couple of minutes.
The only other problem that has always confronted me relates to the role of a member toward his constituents. I know that the people in my constituency want to retain hanging and that I intend to fight against it. This raises problems that all members who want to give effect to the views of their constituents must face. I feel that this is not 23033-248
Division
the kind of subject about which one consults his constituents. This is not the kind of problem such as medicare or the role of the state in planning, about which your constituents have facts upon which you can make decisions.
The problem we face tonight is of the type that can only be settled by study, by reason, by judgment and by experience. This is the type of thing that can never be made available through one's constituents. This would be much like the man on a jury who having heard all the evidence, then goes out on the street and asks the people what he should decide, on the basis of newspaper reports/ There is a time to follow and a time to lead, and during an issue of this kind we face a time when parliament should lead the nation, rather than follow it.
In about one minute we shall take a vote. Speaking for myself, will accept the result whatever it happens to be. I realize that a defeat of the motion will raise very grave and serious problems for the government and certainly for the cabinet. My heart goes out to them because of the agonizing decisions they will have to make.
Having listened to the debate and having received the views of my colleagues in all parts of the house my mind is unchanged. If we are not successful tonight, let me say that we have only lost round one of the battle to take Canada forward, and the fight to abolish the last remnant of this ancient penalty is not dead and has not stopped.
We will begin again tomorrow.

TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING- REQUEST FOR SUBSIDIZATION OF TEACHER TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I asked a question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) concerning the possibility of bringing teacher training under the subsidizing section of the manpower retraining program. I do not think it is necessary for me to point out to hon. members of this house the importance of all matters pertaining to education. At this time of year our newspapers are full of advertisements for teachers, indicating that the chronic shortage of teachers which has been persistent in Canada since the war has not begun to be resolved. I am sure we will all agree, too, that it is a matter of priorities in coming to grips with the general problems of education.
For many years in Canada and in this house there was neglect on the part of the Parliament of Canada and the Government of Canada with respect to responsibilities in the field of education. In recent years there have been major breakthroughs, and particularly I would refer to the technical training program which I believe got under way in 1961.
Since 1961, there has been some $1 billion spent in the construction of new vocational schools. The number of these schools has amounted to 880, and 337,878 new student places have been provided under our Technical and Vocational Training Act. I am sure that this brief review of the statistics will indicate that the problem to which I have referred, that is the shortage of teachers, has been confounded and aggravated by this one program alone.

DEBATES	April 5, 1966
I am sure that it must have been an oversight when this particular aspect of the manpower program was organized to have neglected bringing under the regulations a subsidy provision for teacher training of recruits. It seems to me that it would be particularly helpful to the older worker who has been replaced by a process of automation and technological change, and yet has the necessary educational background, to go on to teacher training college and, within the short space of a year, prepare himself or herself for an entirely new career as well as make a very great contribution to the whole upsurge in our educational program.
This obvious oversight came to my attention when I had several people approach me indicating that they had not been able to come under the subsidy retraining schedule. It was a surprise, I found, to even government officials in the regional national employment offices. They tried in every conceivable way to bend the regulations, realizing the importance of a program of this kind. Unfortunately they just could not accommodate these persons within the present terms of the act. As a result, we were only able to assist these people by having them go on welfare during the period they were under training in a teacher training college.
I think it is significant, Mr. Speaker, that in the United States, which has embarked upon a vast program of war on poverty, one of the new programs contemplated by the President in attacking this problem is the provision of a teacher corps. Teaching is essential to any upgrading program. We have a shortage of teachers. We have people who are willing to enter the profession of teaching. I think it would be of great assistance to them if the regulations could be changed to overcome this unwitting mistake that has been made, and a program provided for preparing teachers for general schools.
Before you can accept students into these vocational schools, of course there must be preliminary education. I am sure, therefore I do not have to go any further in this presentation. In view of the fact that potential retraining candidates are now making plans for training courses next year, I trust that some action can be taken as quickly as possible to resolve this difficulty.

maintopic: TECHNICAL AND VOCATIONAL TRAINING- REQUEST FOR SUBSIDIZATION OF TEACHER TRAINING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has brought many worth-while points to our attention. At the same time I think it should be pointed
April 5, 1966

out that the training of teachers is clearly a provincial responsibility. Although it is part of the joint programs between the federal and provincial governments, the initiative in matters such as this rests with the provinces.
Assistance to the provinces in the training of technical and vocational teachers is provided for under program 7 of the Technical and Vocational Training Agreement. The number of persons trained under this program has increased considerably since 1961. In the past five years, 6,200 persons have been enrolled in teacher training courses under this program. The federal government has contributed $1.6 million to the cost of these courses. Since 1961 new technical and vocational teacher training centres have been established, or existing operations expanded, in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario. The four Atlantic provinces have jointly expanded the technical and vocational teacher training centre at Moncton.
Much of the foregoing increase in teacher training has been oriented to the preparation of technical and vocational teachers for secondary schools. It is true that teacher training for those engaged in the teaching of adults has not been adequately developed, and consideration is now being given to this aspect of the problem.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Some steps have been taken as a result of recommendations made by various organizations interested in this matter. This summer this department, in co-operation with Carleton University, the Northern Electric Company, the National Research Council and other organizations, is arranging a pilot project course designed to upgrade instructors in electronics. The department is also developing a concise package training course that can be used in teaching adults.
The crucial task at the present time is to raise the general level of skills in the labour force through training. While the vocational training of youths coming up through the school system contributes to this objective, it is essential to increase the scale of training among adult workers, and to achieve that requires an increase in the quantity and quality of teachers.
The National Technical and Vocational Training Advisory Council recommended last fall that the minister develop a plan to increase the number of competent teachers and administrators of technical and vocational courses, and to upgrade and retrain technical instructional staff. This recommendation is now being studied by the department.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may 1 add that the observations of the hon. member have been noted and will be brought to the attention of the department for further study.
